primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'T_{\\text{lat}}': 'latency in seconds', 'T_{\\text{ttl}}': 'time-to-live in milliseconds', 'L_{\\text{lic}}': 'licensing status (binary)', 'N_{\\text{norm}}': 'normalization error (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Public domain data, no personal identifiers, deterministic venue mapping.

primitives.assumptions: Aggregate-only data, no individual-level tracking, probabilistic reporting.

primitives.name: Snap Count Aggregation
primitives.verbatim_quote: Each row: category → source class → route → latency → licensing/privacy/ToS → normalization → predictive value (1-10) → falsification test → status of evidence.
primitives.assumptions: Batch-loaded data, normalized to weekly intervals, no real-time updates.

layer2.mapping: Maps snap share and usage pulse to player workload indices via linear regression kernels.
layer2.telemetry: Snap count variance against expected baseline distribution.

Each is governed by a shared lattice of provenance, validity, and normalization fidelity. The failure mode of any primitive—whether due to latency, missingness, or licensing—can cascade into degraded inference in GSI's Bayesian framework. For example, if injury data is missing (M_miss=1), the posterior over player availability collapses, affecting downstream snap count predictions. Similarly, if weather data lacks temporal alignment (timezone mismatch), the predictive model's calibration fails. These primitives must be evaluated under a common TTL (time-to-live) constraint to ensure real-time relevance. The dualities lie in how each primitive encodes uncertainty: weather via stochastic fields, injury via binary indicators, and snap counts via temporal series. The system's robustness depends on maintaining cross-layer coherence and enforcing anti-collinearity among sources to prevent overfitting.
